title: La Belle au bois dormant - Sleeping Beauty in the Wood (తెలుగు)

keywords: la belle au bois dormant - sleeping beauty in the wood
full_text:
In a grand kingdom nestled between rolling green hills and misty pine forests, a noble king and queen long wept for lack of a child. When at last a daughter was born to them, their joy was beyond measure, and they proclaimed a magnificent christening feast that echoed through the marble courtyards of the palace. To bless the royal infant, they invited seven ancient and benevolent fairies who dwelt in the hidden grottos of the realm, bestowing upon each an ornate case of pure gold containing a spoon, knife, and fork wrought of heavy silver and studded with diamonds and rubies.

As the guests took their seats at the banquet table, the great carved oak doors groaned open. An eighth fairy, an elderly crone who had not emerged from her mossy tower in fifty years and was believed by the entire court to be dead or enchanted, hobbled into the hall on an ebony staff. The king hastily bade her welcome, but because only seven golden cases had been crafted, she was given service in fine porcelain and silver. Slighting herself insulted, the old fairy muttered dark venom under her breath as she took her seat.

When the feast ended, the fairies approached the cradle of cedar and silk to bestow their supernatural gifts. The first fairy gave the princess beauty surpassing the petals of the morning rose; the second gave her the spirit and wit of an angel; the third gave her grace in every movement; the fourth gave her the voice of a celestial nightingale; the fifth gave her skill upon the harp and lute; and the sixth gifted her nimble lightness in dance.

Then the vengeful old fairy stepped forward, shaking with spite. Leaning over the cradle, she hissed: 'My gift is this: when the princess is in her sixteenth summer, she shall prick her hand upon the spindle of a spinning wheel, and she shall instantly die!' A chill seized the hall; the queen fainted into the arms of her ladies, and the courtiers wept in despair.

At that moment, a young fairy who had prudently hidden behind the velvet tapestries stepped forth. 'Grieve not, Your Majesties,' she said in a soothing voice like running water. 'My magic cannot wholly overturn the ancient curse, but it can soften its sting. The princess shall not die. When the spindle pricks her tender finger, she shall fall into a deep, peaceful slumber lasting one hundred years, until a king's son arrives to awaken her.'

Desperate to shield his beloved child, the king issued a stern royal decree forbidding any soul in the realm to spin with a spindle or keep a spinning wheel in their dwelling under penalty of death. For fifteen years, the princess grew into radiant grace, beloved by all who beheld her. On the day of her sixteenth birthday, while exploring the upper turrets of a secluded forest chateau, she climbed a winding stone stair and came upon an attic chamber where an honest old peasant woman sat alone, whirring her distaff, having never heard of the king's distant proclamation.

'What are you doing, grandmother?' the girl asked with childlike curiosity. 'May I try the spinning rod?' As she reached out her hand, the whirling wooden needle pricked her fingertip. In an instant, her breath slowed, her eyes closed in peaceful rest, and she sank onto a bed embroidered with gold, asleep in perfect stillness.

The good fairy who had softened the curse arrived in a chariot of fire drawn by winged dragons. Knowing the princess would be terrified to wake alone in a distant century, she touched with her wand every creature in the castle—the royal guards, the lord chamberlain, the maids of honor, the cooks in the kitchen, the spit-turning turnspit dog, and the stallions in the marble stables. All fell into enchanted slumber. Outside, great brambles, dense hawthorns, and towering oaks sprang from the earth, weaving an impassable thicket that concealed the castle towers from mortal sight.

A century passed like a single night. A brave prince from a neighboring dynasty was hunting deer when he saw the ancient stone spires rising above the mysterious forest. An elderly peasant recounted the old legend: that a sleeping princess of unmatched beauty lay within, awaiting the destined royal touch. With courage in his heart, the prince pushed toward the briars; to his wonder, the thorny branches parted like silk curtains, allowing him to pass.

He strode through silent courtyards where guards slept leaning on their halberds and dogs rested with their paws across their noses. Reaching the high gilded chamber, he beheld the princess, whose cheeks still bloomed with the freshness of youth. Overcome with reverence and love, he knelt beside her couch and gently took her warm hand.

Her eyelids fluttered open, her sapphire eyes met his, and she whispered: 'Is it you, my prince? You have kept me waiting long.' At that instant, the spell broke. Roosters crowed, the kitchen spits resumed their turning, the guards saluted, and the chapel bells chimed. Joined in marriage before the assembled court, the prince and princess governed with wisdom and compassion, proving that no darkness of malice can ever extinguish the light of destined hope.
moral: Patience and virtue endure through the longest trials, and true goodness awakens beauty in its appointed time. [TE]
